#2044. Andy Robertson was left with a ‘headache’ after two Liverpool games last season that he ‘hated’

Andy Robertson has said that there were two Liverpool matches in particular last season that he ‘hated’, having been left with a ‘headache’ after both.

The Reds were beaten twice by Galatasaray in the 2025/26 Champions League, with a pair of 1-0 defeats at RAMS Park in the league phase in September and the round of 16 first leg in March (Arne Slot’s team won the return fixture 4-0 a week later).

Both matches were almost clones of one another, with the Merseysiders conceding an early goal and being unable to restore parity after putting in a subdued performance.

Now of Tottenham Hotspur, Robertson reflected on the two visits to Istanbul last season and how he was left with a migraine from the incessant intimidation from the natives.

The Scottish left-back said (via Fanatik): “I hated playing against Galatasaray last season. The Galatasaray away game was terrible. They booed non-stop throughout the entire match. Believe me, you leave the match with a headache.”

Want more Empire of the Kop coverage? Add us as a preferred source on Google to your favourites list for news you can trust

The city of Istanbul has left an indelible mark in Liverpool’s European history from the epic 2005 Champions League final against AC Milan, but recent visits to the Turkish capital have been bruising.

The Reds twice relinquished a lead to lose 3-2 away to Fenerbahce last week, and the two trips to play Galatasaray last season were galling, to say the least.

Pat Nevin justifiably claimed that the 1-0 league phase defeat ‘could have been worse‘ given the nature of our defending that night, and John Aldridge described the repeat of that scoreline in the knockout phase eight months ago as a ‘horrible watch‘.

Slot had warned about the febrile atmosphere of RAMS Park prior to the latter fixture, remarking: “Sometimes you wonder if this could be done by human people”, and for a player of Robertson’s character and experience to be so rattled by the intensity of the home support is quite telling.

With Galatasaray currently 18th in the league phase standings, it’s not inconceivable that they and Liverpool could meet at some point in the knockout rounds yet again next spring, but we’d imagine that the Reds have had their fill of visits to Istanbul after the past 14 months.

#2043. Arsenal face January dilemma as Liverpool and Chelsea join Alex Scott transfer race

Lucie Turner writes about Arsenal for Read Arsenal and Newcastle United for Read Newcastle. A long-time Arsenal supporter, she also follows rugby, snooker, darts and Formula 1. Her work covers match previews and reports, breaking news, player profiles and opinion pieces.

Arsenal have made contact with Bournemouth over a potential move for Alex Scott. Mikel Arteta may have to rethink his transfer plans if competition for the midfielder intensifies.

According to The i Paper, Arsenal, Liverpool and Chelsea have all made exploratory enquiries about the 23-year-old. The clubs want to establish what it would take to persuade Bournemouth to sell. However, none appears close to agreeing to a deal.

Arsenal are believed to be keen on a summer move. Liverpool and Chelsea are more interested in signing Scott in January. However, if they were to make a serious offer, it could be hard to hold out.

Scott has become one of the most exciting midfielders in the Premier League. He is an attractive option for clubs looking to improve their squad going forward due to his age, experience and being a homegrown player.

However, there is some uncertainty around Scott’s future. The England international has turned down two contract offers and is unwilling to sign a new deal. There are 18 months left on Scott’s contract, meaning it is an increasingly important decision for Bournemouth.

Arsenal are interested in Scott with doubts surrounding their own midfield options. There have been reports linking Martin Zubimendi and Mikel Merino to exits.

Scott would give Arteta another option, but Arsenal will have to consider if they want to make a move and give Liverpool and Chelsea an advantage.

Bournemouth are reported to want more than £100m to let him go during the January transfer window.

It would be a big asking price, especially given that Scott has 18 months left on his contract. There are a few reasons why Bournemouth could be holding out for a big fee.

The Cherries had to pay £25m to bring Scott in from Bristol City, who will receive 20 per cent of any future transfer fee. They will also have to find a suitable replacement at the halfway stage.

Reports said Chelsea received a number of offers worth around £70m in the summer, but Bournemouth have rejected claims that a bid of £80m will get them talking.

Scott is believed to be happy to stay at the club until the end of the campaign. Bournemouth are also having a great season under Marco Rose, currently sitting in seventh place in the Premier League with eight straight wins in all competitions.

Arsenal have little to hurry into any deal and could use the summer to negotiate a better deal. This is especially true with Scott’s contract situation becoming more of an issue.

The problem is that Liverpool and Chelsea are keen competitors and could lead to a bidding war in January, leaving Arsenal with little room to negotiate.

Whilst Arsenal have made their interest known, this doesn’t necessarily mean he will be moving anytime soon. If Scott is a genuine target, then they must be prepared to pounce if the situation arises.

#2042. Chelsea news: Stewart departure, Scott interest and Bournemouth preparations

Gary Gowers is a sports journalist and the editor of Read Everton, where he leads daily coverage of Everton news, transfers and analysis. Chelsea’s sporting department is facing another change following news of Laurence Stewart’s impending departure, while the club continue to be linked with potential additions to their squad.

Alex Scott and Palmeiras teenager Eduardo Conceicao have both featured in Thursday’s transfer coverage, with Xabi Alonso also preparing his players for Saturday’s Premier League meeting with Bournemouth.

Here is our 7pm round-up of the latest Chelsea news for Thursday, 8 October.

Laurence Stewart is set to leave Chelsea by mutual consent after almost four years at Stamford Bridge, with the club planning to redistribute his responsibilities rather than appoint a direct replacement.

His departure is understood to be amicable and will not take immediate effect. Stewart joined from Monaco in 2022, initially as technical director, before becoming co-sporting director alongside Paul Winstanley.

As detailed in our report on Stewart’s departure and Chelsea’s leadership reshuffle, Winstanley, Sam Jewell and Joe Shields are expected to take on expanded responsibilities across recruitment, player development and the wider BlueCo operation.

The changes follow discussions about the club’s sporting structure that reportedly began earlier this year. There is no confirmed suggestion that Stewart’s departure resulted from a disagreement with Alonso.

Chelsea’s reported interest in Bournemouth midfielder Alex Scott remains a talking point, despite the south coast club’s determination to retain the England international.

The Blues reportedly had a £64m offer rejected during the summer, with Matt Law of The Telegraph subsequently identifying Chelsea as leading contenders for the 23-year-old.

However, as examined in our latest report on Chelsea’s interest in Scott, Bournemouth are not expected to entertain a January sale.

Scott’s immediate concern is recovering from a thigh injury suffered while representing England. The midfielder could face several weeks on the sidelines, potentially complicating Bournemouth’s plans as well as any future discussions about his next move.

Chelsea have also reportedly made contact with Palmeiras over 16-year-old forward Eduardo Conceicao, who is attracting attention from several leading European clubs.

According to Mark Brus of CaughtOffside, Chelsea have held discussions with the Brazilian club as they explore the possibility of a future deal.

Our report on Chelsea’s interest in Eduardo Conceicao explains that a valuation as high as €100m has been suggested, although that figure is not a confirmed asking price or evidence of a formal bid.

Manchester City, Arsenal and Real Madrid are among the other clubs reportedly monitoring the teenager. Conceicao would be unable to complete a transfer to England until he turns 18, making any prospective move a longer-term consideration.

Alonso’s attention will now turn to Saturday’s Premier League meeting with Bournemouth at Stamford Bridge.

The match kicks off at 3pm and will not be televised live in the United Kingdom because of the Saturday afternoon broadcasting blackout.

Our Chelsea v Bournemouth kick-off and how-to-watch guide provides the full details, including how to follow the match and the available overseas broadcast information.

Scott’s injury is expected to deprive Bournemouth of an important midfield option, although Chelsea will have their own fitness decisions to make as players return from international duty.

After Saturday’s fixture, Chelsea travel to Hill Dickinson Stadium to face Everton on 17 October. Alonso will be looking for greater consistency as the domestic programme resumes.

Lucie Turner writes about Arsenal for Read Arsenal and Newcastle United for Read Newcastle. A long-time Arsenal supporter, she also follows rugby, snooker, darts and Formula 1. Her work covers match previews and reports, breaking news, player profiles and opinion pieces.

Viktor Gyökeres has put to bed any doubts over his future at Arsenal by stating his desire to stay.

The striker has been under question over his long-term future under Mikel Arteta after a difficult start to the 2026/27 season. His latest comments suggest he will not be seeking a move away from north London.

Gyökeres moved to Arsenal for £63.5m from Sporting Lisbon last summer. He’s played a key role in the club winning the Premier League last season with 14 league goals.

However, he has not featured as much this season. Kai Havertz often being Arteta’s go-to man centrally, resulting in him only starting once in the Premier League.

This has led to some speculation that the Sweden international may look at his options in January. However, his latest interview with the Swedish outlet Fotbollskanalen suggests otherwise.

Gyökeres was asked if he wants to stay at Arsenal and has made it clear he wants to continue his career at the Emirates.

The striker also spoke about his relationship with Arteta.

He explained that they regularly discuss football, the team’s approach and the opposition. Those conversations also help him understand what Arteta expects when he is selected to start.

It is a key point to note that just because he hasn’t had much time on the pitch doesn’t mean there have been any issues between the two.

Gyökeres has begun to show his worth again in recent weeks. He found the net against Fleetwood in the League Cup and then Slavia Prague in the Champions League.

This came after a long time to get his first goal of the season and gives him the chance to remind Arteta what he can bring to the team.

There is no doubt that Gyökeres has not lived up to the expectations he had when he came from Portugal.

But his overall effect cannot be ignored. He has contributed 23 goals and 6 assists in 69 games for Arsenal.

The challenge will be finding a way to get the best out of him and Havertz. They add different attributes, and Arteta will have plenty of options to choose from depending on the opposition.

They will also want to avoid losing someone they have invested heavily in so early on. Gyökeres has a contract until 2030, so they are in a great position.

His latest comments will help to reassure fans that he is not looking to leave the club after stating his ambition to play more games and make himself an indispensable part of Arteta’s squad.

The main thing for Arsenal will be to make sure that he can turn this attitude into consistent performances. Gyökeres has made his intentions clear and now needs to show why they brought him to North London in the first place.

#2038. Jussi Jääskeläinen praises Arsenal star David Raya

Lucie Turner writes about Arsenal for Read Arsenal and Newcastle United for Read Newcastle. A long-time Arsenal supporter, she also follows rugby, snooker, darts and Formula 1. Her work covers match previews and reports, breaking news, player profiles and opinion pieces.

Former Premier League goalkeeper Jussi Jääskeläinen thinks David Raya is the best goalkeeper in the division right now.

But the former Bolton Wanderers star feels the Arsenal No.1 has more to prove before he can be put up with the all-time greats of the competition.

Jääskeläinen recently spoke to Kasinopartio.com, where he praised Raya’s performances and the understanding he has developed with Arsenal’s defenders.

“Raya has been a fantastic signing. He has a great relationship with the centre-backs; even when the back four changes, everything works well.”

The Spaniard has played a key role for Mikel Arteta since his arrival from Brentford. His organisation of the backline, key saves and contribution to Arsenal’s build up play have helped him to be a standout player.

In 2012, Raya began his journey in English football when he moved to Blackburn Rovers from Spain. At that time, he was just a young teenager unfamiliar with English football.

His short spell at Southport introduced him to senior football. Soon, he returned to Blackburn and forged a career ahead of moving to Brentford in 2019. After four years with Brentford, Raya achieved success at the club, helping them to the Premier League.

The player’s performances in the higher leagues caught the attention of Arsenal, and Arteta signed him on loan to the Emirates in 2023 before making the move permanent the following summer.

It didn’t take long for Raya to establish himself in the team. He took home the Premier League Golden Glove, having achieved 16 clean sheets in 32 appearances.

This was a significant milestone in his first season with the Arsenal team, and he has since remained as number one, playing a key role in the club’s pursuit of titles.

While Jääskeläinen said Raya is the best goalkeeper in the Premier League at the moment, he does not think he should be up there with the most experienced.

He believes other goalkeepers have earned an advantage through their consistency over a longer period.

“You have lots of top goalkeepers that I think are still a little bit ahead because of the years they’ve done it in the Premier League.”

“He’s not up there with them yet, but he’s definitely going in the right direction.”

Raya has already proven he can play to the top standard. However, it will be his consistency moving forward that will define his long-term reputation.

Petr Čech, Peter Schmeichel and Edwin van der Sar have all gained great reputations over the years. There is still plenty of time for Raya to do the same, but he will need to keep up his high standards whilst wearing an Arsenal shirt.

At just 31, Raya has a lot left in his career. If he can continue playing at this level, it will make the debate around whether he is one of the best goalkeepers in the Premier League even more intriguing.

The newest suggestions from EFL specialist site the72.co.uk suggest Castellanos could be heading back home – however there’s a catch:

“River Plate reportedly view the 28-year-old as a priority target in their striker search, although the finances involved in the deal could prove to be a major hurdle. However, cashing in could give WHUFC the chance to sign a true talisman to aid their promotion bid. “

“Cashing in”? I think not: That’s the elephant in the room here. River Plate have already disclosed that they’ll look at some kind of loan or shared purchase option – as they’re short of funds – which of course will cut no ice with West Ham who will want to replace Taty with a striker more suited to scoring the Championship goals they require.

Merely shipping Taty out on loan without a permanent sale will serve no useful purpose and could actually weaken Scott Parker’s squad. The Hammers have enough loaned – out unwanted stars as it is: Another one added to the list won’t help a rebuild. The only possible route could involve a swap for goal keeper Santiago Beltran – which would still leave the Hammers short of a goal scorer and needing to offload Hermansen or Areola in the winter.

And how often to these player swaps ever come off? Exactly.

From the old Bobby Moore Upper to the Billy Bonds' stand these days - I've been watching since '03 and a supporter since about 1970.. Favourite player - Dean Ashton: Curse you Shaun Wright-Phillips. I still watch YouTube repeats of the Cup Final of 2006 hoping in vain that Shaka Hislop grows another six inches and stops Steven Gerrard's injury time equaliser. Can tell I'm getting old knowing I watched both Mark Noble's debut and his last game at West Ham. Pulling on a Claret and Blue replica shirt still makes me feel the same butterflies as when I was seven years old. Magic.

#2034. Transfer insider outlines Liverpool’s stance on selling Frimpong amid reported Saudi interest

Liverpool could potentially be open to selling Jeremie Frimpong for the right price in 2027, according to one transfer insider.

The Dutchman joined the Reds from Bayer Leverkusen almost 18 months ago and scored on his debut in the Community Shield, but unfortunately his time at Anfield so far has been dogged by several injury absences.

The 25-year-old has been sidelined with a muscle problem he incurred in the victory at Brentford last month, when he was forced off just seven minutes after his introduction as a half-time substitute, whilst he’s also shipped criticism over the nature of some of his performances this term.

According to Pete O’Rourke for Football Insider, Liverpool could ‘consider’ selling Frimpong next year, and the right-back has reportedly been attracting transfer interest from Saudi Pro League outfit Al-Hilal.

The Merseysiders won’t sanction a January exit for the Netherlands international due to concerns over squad depth amid the ongoing long-term absence of Conor Bradley, but club and player could be open to a summer departure if a ‘big offer’ is tabled.

The transfer insider also claimed that Andoni Iraola doesn’t have the strength in depth that he’d like, with the Basque feeling that his squad is lighter than many of the Reds’ direct rivals.

Want more Empire of the Kop coverage? Add us as a preferred source on Google to your favourites list for news you can trust

First things first, there’s no way that Liverpool are in a position to consider offloading Frimpong in January, even if Bradley manages to return by then.

The latter will take time to fully get up to speed after not playing for nearly a whole year, and his own injury history isn’t the most auspicious either.

Ronald Araujo is currently doing an excellent job at right-back, but it isn’t his natural position and it remains to be seen whether or not his loan move from Barcelona will be converted into a permanent transfer.

If that does happen and Bradley rediscovers the strong performance levels that he’d shown prior to his knee injury, maybe then Liverpool would have more scope to consider a substantial offer for Frimpong if he’s not getting much of a look-in under Iraola.

For now, though, the Dutchman is very much needed at Anfield, and hopefully he’ll become available for action once the November international break has concluded towards the end of next week.

#2033. Arsenal Women vs Barcelona: Arsenal show their resilience with impressive draw against Barcelona

Lucie Turner writes about Arsenal for Read Arsenal and Newcastle United for Read Newcastle. A long-time Arsenal supporter, she also follows rugby, snooker, darts and Formula 1. Her work covers match previews and reports, breaking news, player profiles and opinion pieces.

Arsenal Women vs Barcelona: Arsenal Women claimed a vital point at the Camp Nou. They drew 1-1 against Barcelona in the Champions League on Thursday night.

Frida Maanum gave the Gunners the lead in the first half. Caroline Graham Hansen scored to bring the game level after the break. Whilst Renee Slegers will be disappointed to miss out on all three points, her side played some encouraging football.

Despite needing to play differently, Arsenal had an even game against an opposition who would inevitably have long periods of the ball. The visitors played very well defensively and looked dangerous when they could attack.

The result showed that Slegers has a team that can adapt to new challenges. This could be important for Arsenal as they try to make a mark in Europe.

One of the key decisions made by Slegers was to include Maanum. She had only recently returned from injury but made an impressive impact against Barcelona.

The midfielder scored early on to start the game in the right direction. Slegers was very impressed with her play when not in possession. She was praised for her communication skills and assisting others.

Arsenal’s attacking play was mainly based on fast counter attacks. They knew they wouldn’t be able to play in the same style as Barcelona and therefore tried to take advantage of the space on offer.

However, there were chances created in both halves. Arsenal may have been more clinical with their chances, they were always a threat.

Eventually, Barcelona scored their equaliser through Graham Hansen. Slegers said that Arsenal lost their shape during the move, which gave Hansen too much space.

It was a reminder of how quickly Barcelona can strike if you lose your concentration for a moment.

The Arsenal manager was pleased with the way her players implemented the game plan, showing tenacity, discipline, good communication and bravery.

Slegers admitted Arsenal did lose the ball too much in the second half, and by keeping it longer, they would have taken the pressure off defending against Barca’s dangerous attack.

There was some frustration that Arsenal couldn’t hold onto their lead, and there were more chances created towards the end of the game. The visitors got into good positions to win corners but couldn’t get the winning goal.

They will feel very positive from their display. They put themselves up against one of the biggest tests in the Camp Nou and proved that they can cause Barcelona problems.

There isn’t much time to really reflect on the result ahead of their game against the London City Lionesses on Sunday, but Slegers now has another example of what her side can do when they play with purpose and structure.

#2029. Why England fans booed Arsenal defender Ben White again after Croatia win

Lucie Turner writes about Arsenal for Read Arsenal and Newcastle United for Read Newcastle. A long-time Arsenal supporter, she also follows rugby, snooker, darts and Formula 1. Her work covers match previews and reports, breaking news, player profiles and opinion pieces.

Ben White returned to the England senior squad on Thursday night but received a hostile reception at Wembley.

The Arsenal defender came on as a substitute in the 78th minute of England’s 2-1 Nations League win against Croatia but was met with boos from a section of the crowd.

Thomas Tuchel has since defended White, stating that he should be in the squad. However, this raises questions as to why some England supporters have turned on the defender after he has continued to perform well for Arsenal.

The answer lies with the 2022 World Cup in Qatar.

He did not play in the first two group games for England and missed the last group game against Wales due to illness.

There were reports that White had fallen out with assistant manager Steve Holland, but neither the FA nor England management confirmed this was the reason he left.

Gareth Southgate later stated there were no problems between White and Holland and that White had simply withdrawn himself from selection after the tournament.

This meant that White would never play for England again while Southgate was still manager. Some fans were clearly upset by this, as they felt White was shunning his country.

When White returned under Tuchel in March 2026, he was met with a negative reaction. He was booed by the crowd when he scored his first-ever international goal against Uruguay. White was also booed in the same fashion against Japan.

He has since explained that supporters might view the situation differently if they knew the full story. However, he has chosen not to reveal the private details behind his departure.

Tuchel has shown little concern about White being affected by the controversy.

The England boss said after the win on Thursday that he had not heard any boos and praised White’s qualities, work ethic and desire to play for his country.

He believes White can help England win games and added that he has the backing of the coaching staff.

Arsenal fans will be unsurprised to learn that White is still a valuable asset for Mikel Arteta, offering defensive consistency and being able to play as a right or centre-back.

The bad press that White is receiving from England fans will not go away any time soon. However, he has not done anything to hurt his reputation at club level. The reasons why he left for the World Cup are personal.

The main focus for Arsenal will be getting him match fit again. As for the England fans, we shall see.

#2028. Ten things I hate about football (Part One)

The independent voice of Newcastle United since 1988

Get your daily update and weekly newsletter by signing up today!

Get your daily update and weekly newsletter by signing up today!

From my view it’s THE great game, though cricket, proper Test cricket, runs a close second in a league table of sporting passions.

How can anyone remain unmoved by the heart-pounding excitement, the last-minute goals, the balletic skills, the blood and thunder, the thud and blunder of the beautiful game? The beauty is in the simplicity: outscoring the opposition makes you the better team, on that day at least.

Increasingly, however, elite-level football is finding ways to make a pig’s ear of a silk purse.

The latest international break, which I reckon means we have endured five fallow weeks already this season after only 10 rounds of Premier League fixtures, has allowed time to reflect on what really gets my goat.

Most of the ire is directed at recent developments, a trend that suggests change is not synonymous with progress. So here they are, the first five of 10 things I hate about football. Those who know me, even tangentially, will be unsurprised I’m chuntering like a grumpy old man even before kick-off.

As soon as the players head back to the dressing rooms after an energetic warm-up, a veritable deluge soaks the grass.

The protagonists have presumably chosen a stud-length most suited to the surface they have just tested. What a brilliant idea, altering it with the match only minutes away. To raise the probability of players losing their balance (witness Barca v NUFC last season), the deluge is repeated at half-time. Premier League pitches are today usually a blend of turf and plastic, which has all but eliminated the spectacular divots that were once commonplace. Check a video of the 1970 FA Cup final for evidence. Or any match in any season at the old Baseball Ground from November onwards.

So, divots are essentially consigned to history. Hurrah! That doesn’t explain the obsession with soaking the surface. My best guess is that a wet pitch allows the goalscorer to indulge in an elongated double-knee slide without risk of doing an ACL. Such celebrations are tosh. Stop this waste of water right now. Bring back the gentlemanly brief handshake or, if you must, go wild and slap the hero heartily on the back.

To quote James Taylor, “I’ve seen fire and I’ve seen rain . . . ”

Having with luck banished the artificial rain, let’s ditch the absurd flames that are propelled skywards, seemingly before every Premier League kick-off. When the players emerge from the tunnel and line-up for the officially approved preliminaries, half-a-dozen hefty boxes packed with flammable gas are dragged onto the pitch. Are the pyrotechnics designed to “add to the atmosphere” in other than the physical sense? If so, they are a damp squib. The Premier League’s green credentials are literally incinerated by these pointless rituals.

A waste of time and space is bad enough. It becomes far worse if you are a veteran of armed conflict, witnessing this dire spectacle at the match closest to Remembrance Day. Could anything be a less fitting accompaniment to the ceremonial silence? Some of the servicemen and servicewomen who take part in the tributes to the fallen are probably all too familiar with the damage flames can do.

Ban the pyrotechnics from Premier League grounds, in early November at least. And if our lords and Masters (geddit) say no and insist on wasting fossil fuels throughout the rest of the season, the musical soundtrack has to be Fire, that groovy track from 1968 by The Crazy World of Arthur Brown. Dig that cool Hammond organ, man. It was undoubtedly the finest hour of Vincent Rodney Cheesman aka Vince Crane.

Finally, the match begins, though not as it did in the good old days. When I were a lad, the half-way line separated the teams; 11 players to the left of it, 11 to the right. On the referee’s whistle, the ball had to be kicked forward one full circumference or more. The opponents were allowed no nearer than the perimeter of the centre circle (what on earth would Chelsea’s prima donnas think?!) until the ball was in motion.

In 2016 the law was changed. Although encroachment by opponents is still banned, the player kicking off can stand in their half and, even worse, kick the ball towards his own keeper rather than forwards. No wonder so much play today resembles the aimless wanderings of a cast of crabs intoxicated by putrid kelp.

And there’s more. If an opponent shows the temerity to pursue the back pass, he will find his path blocked by one or more players from the team in possession, who blatantly obstruct his run, grab his shirt or otherwise commit a foul. Those dirty blockers have no intention of playing the ball; their only pathetic ambition is to prevent an opponent from doing so. The day a referee (more on them later) penalises that offence, I’ll believe in an interventionist god.

The prospect of a laughable own goal being scored direct from the kick-off was eliminated at the same time the backwards kick-off was approved. If the ball did enter the net of the team kicking off, without touching a second player, a corner would be awarded to their opponents. Who said the game’s regulators were not killjoys?

Good riddance to some aspects of Seventies football in England, such as the reckless tackle from behind that could end a player’s season or sometimes his career.

What has been the unforeseen consequence, however, when a defender is determined to usher the ball out of play for a goal kick or throw to his side? Again, he has no intention of being directly involved in the play. He is simply hell bent on stopping his opponent. knowing the days are long gone of responding to such tactics with a hefty boot to the posterior. If the attacking player does manage with nimble footwork to jink within touching distance of the ball, what happens? Yes, the defender pushes him in the back, often with both hands, sending him head first into the hi-tech advertising hoardings. Tell me why this is not a foul, Mr Howard Melton Webb MBE.

Keepers were banned from handling the ball if it was deliberately passed to them (via a boot or a throw-in) 34 years ago. The game’s regulators wanted to reduce timewasting. A noble idea, I’m sure you agree. I foolishly hoped outfield players would be discouraged from continually passing the ball back whence it came. No such luck. In many games, the player with the most touches is the No1. Call me old fashioned . . . but I go to football matches to see moments of skill I never dreamed were possible. Breathtaking full-length saves, yes. Fancy footwork by the custodian, no.

In my day, you ended up in goal if your lower limbs were lacking such basic requirements as speed and balance. If you had “an educated left foot”, you were almost bound to be a midfield schemer. A player with vision would be an inside forward (a No10 in today’s parlance). The speedster could go on the wing, either in attack or defence. If you were tall, agile, brave, foolhardy even, then you were going in nets.

The job description does not include an ability to demonstrate a Cruyff turn. Neither should it; except that your cowardly teammates constantly pass the buck when under pressure, kicking the ball back to the keeper instead of accepting the sporting challenge of retaining possession themselves by using their innate ability.

This can, admittedly, lead to a comedic outcome if the keeper overplays his hand, such as when Mark Flekken believed Big Nick Woltemade was slower than slow in the Champions League tie at the BayArena last December. When BNW took the ball off the keeper’s toe and was clattered, Anthony Gordon stepped up to drill home the penalty kick.

That incident was, in the great scheme of things, an oasis of happiness amid a desert of dire back passing, however. The ball-playing keeper has become a get-out-of-jail-free card for teammates who lack the will or skill to take the initiative.

While we’re at it, is there any way of preventing the tippy-tappy nonsense that involves sideways and backwards passes in a team’s defensive penalty area? At the risk of channelling my inner Jack Charlton, get the ball up the bloody pitch! You might just score . . .

Grateful thanks if you’re still reading. Part two is likely to include referees, fixture lists, television and financial chicanery.

#2027. Arsenal Women vs London City Lionesses preview: Gunners face tough test at the Emirates

Lucie Turner writes about Arsenal for Read Arsenal and Newcastle United for Read Newcastle. A long-time Arsenal supporter, she also follows rugby, snooker, darts and Formula 1. Her work covers match previews and reports, breaking news, player profiles and opinion pieces.

Arsenal look to build on their recent win over Liverpool as they return to the Emirates Stadium but will face an impressive London City Lionesses side who are a potent attacking threat on their travels.

Renée Slegers’ team have struggled to convert their strong performances into points in the league this season. They have lost their last four WSL games at home, however, becoming the first team in WSL history to draw four successive games at home.

Their bad run must come to an end. They have taken just three points from their first nine league games so far this season, scoring a miserable total of 10 goals. However, they look like they have more in the tank and will need to be much more clinical in front of the goal.

The day also marks Slegers’ 50th game in charge of the WSL. The Dutch manager has only lost six league games so far this season, with only Chelsea having a better record from teams that have been ever-present in the division.

Arsenal can’t take their opposition lightly after London City’s impressive recent form. They have won two and drawn once in their last three away league games, scoring 12 goals.

Eder Maestre’s side has become a potent attacking force. Daniëlle van de Donk has provided four assists this season, and Delphine Cascarino has scored three goals and provided two assists.

Kadidiatou Diani can be dangerous. She has scored or assisted in all four of her league games away from home this season.

London City’s attacking prowess means they are a far different proposition to some teams Arsenal have faced at home. They have been in a positive situation for 62.7 per cent of their league minutes this season, the highest in the WSL.

Arsenal will have to deal with the attacking threats but look to utilise their ball possession better. Giving London City an opportunity to counter could make an already tough afternoon even tougher.

Alessia Russo comes into the game having found the net in her last three WSL games and will be key in converting Arsenal’s chances into goals.

The Gunners also showed their fighting spirit in their midweek clash against Barcelona. They drew 1-1 at Camp Nou to become the first side to take points off the Spanish giants in the Women’s Champions League at home since April 2024.

Slegers’ team will feel emboldened by that result but will have to change their tactics against London City.

They have won all seven games against Arsenal so far, scoring an impressive 22 goals and only conceding once. However, given London City’s recent away form, they will be hotly favoured.

They certainly have the quality to take all three points, but they must finally convert their dominance into a comfortable home win.

Malick Thiaw looked excellent last season for Newcastle United when arriving in summer 2025 from AC Milan but mistakes started creeping in at times during the final months of a tough 58 game season, when too much was probably asked of the defender due to so many injuries.

#2025. ‘If I stayed…’ – Rio Ngumoha reflects on ‘no-brainer’ decision to swap Chelsea for Liverpool

Rio Ngumoha has said that his decision to swap Chelsea for Liverpool in 2024 was a ‘no-brainer’.

The Reds signed the teenage winger from the London club’s academy just after he turned 16, with a subsequent tribunal determining that the Merseysiders were to pay an initial £2.8m (potentially rising to £6.8m) in compensation.

The now 18-year-old has gone on to make 44 appearances and counting for LFC’s first team, along with winning three senior England caps, and he’s turned in some man-of-the-match performances at Champions League level.

In a recent media interview (via The Standard), Ngumoha explained that he decided to leave Chelsea for Liverpool because he saw a clearer pathway to the first team at Anfield than he did in west London.

The winger said: “I needed a new challenge. I feel like if I stayed at Chelsea… not saying I wouldn’t have got to the first team as quickly, because I believe in my ability, but I feel Liverpool just gave me a new pathway.

“The plan they set for me was straightforward. For me, it was a no-brainer going to Liverpool.”

Want more Empire of the Kop coverage? Add us as a preferred source on Google to your favourites list for news you can trust

The Reds have had a fine track record for attracting top-class teenage talents in recent years, and Ngumoha is perhaps the standout signing in that category.

That Liverpool were prepared to go through a rigorous registration process with the Premier League (as the winger was a minor at the time) shows just how determined they were to see the deal through, and all of that bureaucratic effort has proven to be more than worth it.

In little more than a year, the teenager has gone from highly-rated prospect to established first-team presence, and there’s a palpable excitement among the fans at Anfield every time he gets the ball, with many a defender bamboozled by his phenomenal dribbling ability and supreme self-confidence.

Ngumoha’s leap of faith in joining the Reds has been vindicated by his regularity of senior football, especially this season as he’s started almost half of our matches across all competitions, and full credit to him for seizing his opportunity when it’s been handed to him.

Chelsea’s loss has very much proven to be our gain, and with the 18-year-old now holding a market value of €50m (£41.8m), that aforementioned compensation fee looks increasingly like one of the steals of the century.

#2024. Arsenal transfer interest in Alphadjo Cisse: Arsenal face a £50m decision as AC Milan youngster attracts Premier League interest

Lucie Turner writes about Arsenal for Read Arsenal and Newcastle United for Read Newcastle. A long-time Arsenal supporter, she also follows rugby, snooker, darts and Formula 1. Her work covers match previews and reports, breaking news, player profiles and opinion pieces.

Arsenal transfer interest in Alphadjo Cisse is starting to take shape. Arsenal are monitoring the development of AC Milan starlet Alphadjo Cissé, although his sensational start to the season could prove to be costly for Mikel Arteta.

The 20-year-old has made a blistering start to his Serie A career and attracted interest from a number of Premier League clubs after his impressive displays so far. Arsenal are reported to be interested.

The Gunners are among several clubs, including Brighton, keeping tabs on the player, according to Italian football news website Tuttomercatoweb. The striker is rumoured to be worth up to 60 million euros. That’s an eye-watering sum for a player who is just starting out in his professional career.

Cissé was signed by Milan from Hellas Verona in February 2026 but was allowed to finish the season on loan at Catanzaro.

Prior to joining the San Siro, he had already showcased his potential with six goals in 22 games in Serie B. He has made a huge impact since moving up to the top division.

Cissé has found the net five times in nine Serie A games this season. He has also chipped in with three goals in four Europa League games, making a total of eight goals in 13 games.

This has made him an important addition to the Milan squad. He is also versatile, as he can play as an attacking midfielder or higher up the park.

Arsenal may find his versatility attractive. Arteta likes players who can play in different positions and with injuries, and with a busy fixture list, he will want to have players who can do that.

The main issue could be that Milan are keen to keep their young star.

It is reported that the Italian club have turned down a verbal offer from Brighton and are looking to extend Cissé’s contract, which currently runs until June 2030.

This indicates that Milan is considering his future, rather than looking to make a profit. It also demonstrates just how quickly his reputation has developed.

Arsenal have the funds to target exciting young talent, but would they want to spend so much on Cissé?

There is no indication that he would be an instant replacement for Arsenal’s current attacking options. However, Cissé’s age, goal-scoring ability and versatility make him an interesting prospect.

This could be one to keep an eye on beyond January. Milan have little motivation to sell, and Arsenal might want to see how he develops before committing themselves.

Cissé has already hit the ground running in Italy and now needs to prove that his initial success can turn into something more consistent.

#2020. ‘Unlikely to be…’ – Journalist sounds contract renewal warning over Van Dijk and Alisson

Liverpool fans have been advised that prospective contract renewals for Virgil van Dijk and Alisson Becker could take time to materialise.

The future of both long-serving players has been in the spotlight this week after they publicly addressed their respective situations, with the goalkeeper’s agent already in talks with club chiefs while the captain has maintained a more neutral ‘let’s see’ stance.

Their current deals are set to expire next June, and they’ll be able to sign pre-contract agreements with overseas clubs from the beginning of January unless they extend their terms with the Reds before then.

In an article for The Athletic discussing the futures of Van Dijk and Alisson, James Pearce warned that ‘there is unlikely to be a quick resolution’ to either player’s contract situation, citing how renewals for the Dutchman and Mo Salah two seasons ago weren’t confirmed until April 2025.

The journalist explained how Liverpool would need to take a pragmatic approach to the renewal process and not be led by sentiment, with the defender turning 36 next July and the goalkeeper’s 35th birthday coming three months later.

In a more hopeful note, Pearce wrote: ‘It makes sense for all parties to wait and see how things unfold in the coming weeks and months. Respect abounds and relationships are strong, with dialogue ongoing between sporting director Julian Ward and the pair’s camps.’

Want more Empire of the Kop coverage? Add us as a preferred source on Google to your favourites list for news you can trust

The case studies of Van Dijk and Salah from 2024/25 indicate that we ought not to expect a swift resolution to the current contract situations regarding the Dutchman and Alisson, with negotiations set to involve substantial back-and-forth before any agreement is struck.

Considering ther importance on the pitch, they’re two of the highest-earning players in the current Liverpool squad, with the captain leading the way on £350,000 per week and the goalkeeper pocketing a weekly wage of £250,000 (Capology).

For their deals to be renewed, it’d either take a significant deflection from club policy to hand out lucrative extensions to players in their mid-30s, or the pair to accept a reduction on their base salary and increase the value of performance-related bonuses on offer.

In truth, the contract negotiations for Van Dijk and Alisson will likely run for another few months, and there could be some frayed nerves among Kopites if either or both situations were still unresolved by spring.

However, with the duo proving this season that they remain top-class performers bringing some crucial stability to a much-changed team, Ward must make every effort to keep them at Anfield for at least another year, and we’re cautiously optimistic that both will remain Reds players going into the 2027/28 campaign.

#2019. To infinity and beyond! Another stunning Diego Gomez strike has Brighton up to SECOND and daring to dream... as Brentford's Igor Thiago is goaded into a red card

Published: 11:08 EST, 8 November 2026 | Updated: 12:40 EST, 8 November 2026

Onwards and upwards go Brighton. Another victory to send them soaring into second place with only Arsenal above them.

It is a lofty perch for the Seagulls and one more admirable when considering the depths from which they have risen.

Homeless and penniless, on the brink of extinction at the end of the last century they are now daring to dream about the Champions League.

To infinity and beyond. Why not? Fabian Hurzeler’s team have already beaten Arsenal and Manchester City without conceding this season.

The only goals scored against them in the last six Premier League games came at Liverpool, where they lost 2-0 but were not outplayed.

City’s season is mired in uncertainty, awaiting sentence for financial breaches and the other half of the traditional Big Six are so erratic there will likely be scope for interlopers when the prized European tickets are handed out in May.

It is six months away but at this moment in time there are not four teams better than Fabian Hurzeler’s.

Brighton appear fully formed. Delightfully fluent in attack. Creative with zip and imagination and different ways to score goals.

There is a defined style of play. Solid at the back with enough sporting maturity to survive a test of needle, which this became against Brentford after the red card for Igor Thiago’s red card.

Diego Gomez celebrated another memorable strike at the Amex Stadium after his halfway-line stunner in the 5-0 win over Crystal Palace

The Bees already trailed to a screamer from the left boot of Diego Gomez and went further behind before half time when Pascal Gross converted a penalty awarded for a shirt pull by Keane Lewis-Potter on Luka Vuskovic.

Brighton (4-2-3-1): Verbruggen 6; Costinha 6, Dunk 6, Vuskovic 6, Boscagli 7; Gross 8, Andres 6 (Wieffer 46, ); Gomez 7 (Yalcoue 90+3), Ayari 7 (Hinshelwood 78), De Cuyper 7 (Minteh 82); Kostoulas 6 (Rutter 82)

Subs not used: Steele, Hadjam, Kadioglu, Svoboda

Bookings: Andres, Boscagli, Wieffer, Dunk

Brentford (4-3-3): Kelleher 6; Kayode 5, Ajer 6, Van den Berg 6 (Wilson 70), Lewis-Potter 5 (Diouf 59); Sangare 5 (Jensen 59), Janelt 5, Hickey 5 (Collins 46); Ouattara 4 (Yarmoliuk 46), Thiago 3, Schade 4

Subs not used: Valdimarsson, Anthony, Damsgaard, Schuster

Gross, the 35-year-old midfielder schemer who walloped his penalty into the top corner in emphatic fashion, embodies the confidence pulsing through this team and his goal closed the contest.

The Bees assembled in the deep looking to minimise damage with an eye on a counterattack or a set piece and maybe hoping the officials would see fit to even it up at 10 against 10.

It didn’t happen. Instead, Brighton controlled the ball. They have had more than 75 per cent of possession across 90 minutes and spent the second half probing around the fringes of the Brentford penalty area.

They registered 20 shots in all but there would be no third goal. And nobody minded. They celebrated the victory and a return to the Amex Stadium after five away games in a row and more than 5,000 miles on the road.

Every substitution made by Hurzeler came as a reminder of their strength and quality.

Kaoru Mitoma, yet to feature this season, is expected back from injury soon after the international break.

The Conference League is not proving a distraction to a squad of such depth and Hurzeler gave fans his permission to dream.

'They should be always excited,' said the Brighton boss. 'That’s our job. They can dream. They can have high expectations, but these are things we can’t control. We played good game but always things we can do better.'

This was Brentford’s second defeat in this Premier League season and they had players sent off in both.

'In both scenarios the opposition player has been the one to provoke the situation, antagonise our player and react towards our player in an aggressive way,' fumed boss Keith Andrews, referring to Yehor Yarmoliuk’s red card against Liverpool, when the Bees finished the game with nine men.

'We should do better, but the game is in a state now and a place I don’t particularly like. And we’ll have to have a look at that because it’s costing us.'

Chema Andres fouled Thiago, fell to the ground and sprang up to confront the Brazilian, who tried to push him away but caught him with a forearm under the jaw.

Igor Thiago's yellow card was upgraded to red after a VAR intervention

Andres collapsed for a second time. When Michael Oliver gave them a yellow card each it seemed fair, but VAR Stuart Attwell sent the referee to the pitch-side screens for a review.

Oliver studied the slow-motion replays and upgraded it to a red card. Off went Thiago, smiling wryly and shaking his head, dismissed for standing his ground and being goaded into a reaction.

He will miss games against Everton, Manchester United and Arsenal.

Opinions of Oliver in the away end did not improve when he gave a penalty for a shirt pull by 5ft 7in Keane Lewis-Potter which somehow sent 6ft 4in Luka Vuskovic somersaulting to the turf.

Vuskovic is already a favourite at the Amex Stadium and it is easy to forget he is only 19. He dominates in the air and reads the game like a seasoned central defender.

And after ten games he is ten points better off than those he left behind at Tottenham.

The Croatia international cannot be looking forward to yet another encounter with England. The two nations meet at Wembley on Thursday. England have put 11 past them in two games this year.

#2017. Arteta named as by far the worst nightmare manager to deal with by former top referee

The independent voice of Newcastle United since 1988

Get your daily update and weekly newsletter by signing up today!

Get your daily update and weekly newsletter by signing up today!

Mikel Arteta has been named as by a distance the worst manager to deal with by a former top referee.

Zero surprise to anybody that the Arsenal boss has been named and shamed.

The embarrassing antics of Mikel Arteta on the touchline are there for all to see, as well as his behaviour in interviews and press conferences.

Never mind what he whispers in the ear and we can’t hear, as well as behind closed doors.

The naming and shaming of Mikel Arteta comes from former top Premier League referee Graham Scott.

He was speaking on the Athletic FC podcast in a conversation with Emma Paton, Dan Kilpatrick and Tim Spiers.

Emma Paton asking Graham Scott: “Who was the worst manager to deal with on the touchline?”

The former Premier League referee replying: “Well, the trite answer is: all of them when they’re losing. The honest answer, I’m afraid, I know whatever I say at this point just gets me pelters, but it is Mikel Arteta. He is the hardest work. He really does push all the limits all of the time. I don’t mind that in many ways; he’s trying to get a competitive advantage for his team. That’s fine. That’s part of his job. And of course, he’s entitled to do it, and it’s for us to place them, but he does make your life extremely difficult.”

Graham Scott going on to explain: “He’s out of his box (technical area) all the time. I watched him recently in Arsenal’s game against Everton and every time Everton had the ball anywhere near the touchline on his side, he was like joining in the press — his toes are on the touchline. As fourth official, it’s a nightmare, because if you step forward and do anything about it, you’re being pedantic, being petty. He does get away with rather too much. The officials do need to be a bit tighter. And I was one of them who let him do that. I’m not going to deny that. But he was just hard work. Really, really hard work all the time in a way that others tended to be hard work some of the time.”

#2016. “I don’t know why…” – John Aldridge fears Liverpool’s stance on one player could ‘backfire’

John Aldridge has questioned why Liverpool weren’t more assertive in pulling Dominik Szoboszlai out of national team duty when he’s currently nursing a minor injury.

The midfielder sprained his ankle in the 3-1 victory at Crystal Palace on Sunday, with Andoni Iraola uncertain after the game as to whether or not the 26-year-old would join up with his country during this international window.

In a statement on Tuesday, the Hungarian FA said that a decision on the player’s participation against Georgia and Northern Ireland over the next week will be deferred until the ‘last minute’ as his fitness continues to be assessed.

In his latest column for the Liverpool Echo, Aldridge voiced his belief that Liverpool should’ve done more to prevent Szoboszlai from playing for Hungary in the coming days when he’s clearly not fully fit.

The former Reds striker wrote: ‘I know Virgil van Dijk has pulled out of the Netherlands squad because of a little niggle, but Dominik Szoboszlai has stayed with Hungary despite injuring his knee against Palace.

‘Any other club would pull them out of international duty. Manchester United, Arsenal, Man City – they’d all pull them. We’ve seen it before. Any doubt and that’s it, decision made, you’re not playing. I don’t understand why we don’t throw our weight around like that.

‘I understand players want to play for their country. I was the same with Ireland. I would answer call-ups even when I was injured. I get what it means and how much it means to players, but any other club would just pull them. That’s not happened here, I don’t know why. Hopefully that just means it’s not that serious.

‘It still sounds like they’re taking a risk. If he stays with Hungary and plays, we’ve just got to hope the decision doesn’t backfire and come back to hurt Liverpool.’

Want more Empire of the Kop coverage? Add us as a preferred source on Google to your favourites list for news you can trust

As Szoboszlai is contracted to Liverpool, the Merseyside club could’ve blocked him from representing his country during this international window because of his knee injury.

However, it’d appear to be a case of the player wanting to at least link up with the Hungary camp and try to prove his fitness, and Anfield chiefs green-lighting that action out of respect for the 26-year-old and not wanting to antagonise him by forbidding him to travel.

The grey area over the midfielder potentially being fit enough to play but not certain of doing so has presented a tricky dilemma, as much as Iraola would no doubt have preferred for our number 8 to swerve national team duty and prioritise his club instead.

With Hungary not playing until Saturday, that does give Szoboszlai a bit of time to recover from the knee issue he incurred at Selhurst Park, and we’d like to think that Marco Rossi wouldn’t risk fielding him against Georgia unless he’s definitely OK to feature.

While a swift return to action for the 26-year-old would obviously be a good thing, we just hope it doesn’t come at the expense of his involvement for Liverpool in the coming weeks, especially with a hectic run of 11 matches in 40 days before the end of December.

Welcome to our Live Comments section, where new comments will appear automatically

It is all very well and good for pundits (code word for writers with preposterous assertions) to voice the opinion that LFC should have been more assertive in voicing their opinion on Szoboszlai not starting for Hungary. The problem with that line of thinking is that Szobo is always passionate to play for his country (and as seen last year in his performances to play for LFC), so if you deny him the right to play, you run the risk of alienating him, something Aldridge does not have to concern himself with because he has nothing to do with LFC or Szobo. I also worry that if he is allowed to start when not fit he will further injure himself, but believe Szobo and his manager will not take that action if he is not fit and can understand that Szobo as his country’s captain, if he does not start he would at least like to be on the sidelines giving his teammates moral support – something Aldridge also does not have to concern himself with! The Mag Podcast Episode 16: Newcastle United 2008-09 Chaos, Kevin Keegan and Relegation

Published: 13/11/2026 | Duration: 51 mins | Hosts: Jamie Smith, Simon Cahill & David Hutchinson

In Episode 16 of The Mag Pod, we find Jamie, Simon, and Hutch discussing relegation! Special focus is on the 2008-09 season when the combined efforts of Mike Ashley and Dennis Wise forced Kevin Keegan out and a drop to the Championship was the eventual result. So how does the current 2026-27 NUFC situation compare…?

You can play episode 16 on the audio player above or use your favourite podcast platforms including Spotify, Apple Podcasts, Amazon Music, YouTube, and Acast.

Listen to the latest episode of The Mag Pod! Join Jamie, Simon, and Hutch for unfiltered football debate.

Newcastle United’s disastrous 2008-09 relegation season is back under the microscope as Jamie Smith, Simon Cahill and David Hutchinson revisit the chaos of Kevin Keegan’s departure, Mike Ashley’s ownership and Alan Shearer’s desperate rescue mission.

With Newcastle struggling for consistency in the 2026/27 Premier League season, the lads ask whether history offers any lessons for the current squad – and whether today’s concerns really compare with one of the club’s most turbulent campaigns.

The international break provides a welcome breather from Newcastle’s league struggles, and there’s time for a typically entertaining round up of international action, including Dan Burn and Lewis Hall representing England and Yoane Wissa finding the net for DR Congo. Managerial upheaval elsewhere in the Premier League also provides plenty of ammunition, particularly Manchester United’s latest troubles.

Then it’s back to 2008-09, when optimism surrounding Keegan’s return quickly unravelled into protests, questionable transfers and a succession of managerial changes.

Jamie recalls the toxic atmosphere following the exit of Kevin Keegan, the controversial roles of Dennis Wise and Tony Jimenez, and the extraordinary collection of players who somehow ended up relegated.

From Shay Given’s departure and Joe Kinnear’s eventful spell to Alan Shearer’s arrival with just eight matches remaining, the discussion explores where Newcastle’s season went wrong. There’s also time to remember some miserable away trips, controversial refereeing decisions and the players who eventually helped restore pride in the Championship.

Crucially, the lads compare that relegated side with Newcastle’s current squad, examining leadership, creativity, commitment and the importance of stability. Could the same mistakes happen again, or are today’s foundations considerably stronger?

With more historical comparisons planned throughout the international break, this opening instalment combines painful memories, plenty of gallows humour and a surprisingly reassuring perspective on Newcastle United’s present predicament.

#2014. Marco Rose's Bournemouth should not have the depth to win this many games domestically and abroad but at Ipswich they showed they can do it the hard way, writes JAMES SHARPE

Published: 11:20 EST, 8 November 2026 | Updated: 12:48 EST, 8 November 2026

Juggling domestic duties with European adventures should not be as manageable as this for teams like Bournemouth.

Clubs of their size should be creaking under the weight of the extra fixtures. All those games, all that travelling. They have played nine games in a month.

Far bigger outfits have toiled spinning those plates. Remember when Ange Postecoglou stopped bothering about the Premier League entirely just to focus on the Europa League.

And yet here are those brilliant Cherries, three days after a win in Prague in that same competition, making it eight on the bounce with a victory at Ipswich thanks to Evanilson's opener, following goalkeeper Christian Walton's early howler, and an own goal from Leif Davis.

Bournemouth haven't done that since 2013 when they were getting out of League One.

Now, they are seventh in the Premier League, second in the Europa League.

Leif Davies reacts after scoring an own goal to make it 2-0 to Bournemouth

And they're in the League Cup quarter-finals – all while having the squad depth to name Alex Scott and Junior Kroupi on the bench.

Marco Rose's side showed they can also do it the hard way, too, after Jack Clarke's second-half penalty for Ipswich, given for a soft foul on Abdoul Ouattara, provided a far more tense final 15 minutes than anticipated inside a feverish Portman Road where Julio Enciso also twice went close from late free-kicks.

'One goal changed the momentum of the game and that's why I'm much more pleased about the last 20 minutes because we suffered but we did it together,' said Rose.

First James Trafford, now Walton. Bournemouth's win over Leeds last weekend also hinged on a goalkeeping howler, when Trafford's simple pass out from the back was intercepted.

This time Ipswich stalwart Walton took a back pass from Dara O'Shea and decided the best course of action was to try to dummy and turn Evanilson. He failed, of course.

Evanilson rolled the ball into an empty net. That intense Bournemouth press really can do some crazy things to you.

IPSWICH (4-2-3-1): Walton 4; Ouattara 5, Diop 6, O'Shea 6, Davis 5; Florentino 7 (Akpom 85), Palacios 6; Maeda 6 (Fatawu 65, 7), Enciso 7; Philogene 6 (Clarke 54, 7); Emersonn 5 (Flemming 54, 6)

BOURNEMOUTH (4-2-3-1): Petrovic 6; Smith 6 (Diakite 79), Hill 7, Silva 7; Truffert 7; Adams 7, Christie 6 (Cook 67, 5); Rayan 6 (Adli 86), Kluivert 6 (Kroupi 68, 6), Tavernier 7; EVANILSON 8 (Rodriguez 85)

After scoring the opener in Bournemouth's win last weekend, manager Marco Rose told Evanilson that he was becoming a 'real No9'.

That's six goals now in his last seven games but it's his all-round play that's so impressive.

He dropped in and played a beautiful curling through ball into the channel to set Justin Kluivert free down the right.

He collected the loose ball for the second goal.

He made a fine run to latch on to a free-kick over the defence to stab the ball over to James Hill at the back post, who headed over from close range, which would have put him level with Declan Rice as the leading assister in the league too.

'He's so hard-working,' added Rose. 'He does everything out of possession.

'He starts the press, he plays in between the lines, he gives us deep runs.

'But the most important thing is scoring and he understood that he also needs to arrive close to goal if he wants to score.'

If the Tractor Boys are to make their stay in the Premier League a longer one than last time, they cannot afford to keep giving early leads. The mountain is steep enough.

Evanilson's opener was the sixth time Ipswich have conceded inside the first 15 minutes of a league game this season. They are yet to score one that early.

A howler from Ipswich keeper Christian Walton gifted Evanilson the opener

James Hill celebrates Bournemouth's win which lifts them to seventh

It is what will make this defeat especially frustrating for Gary O'Neil against his former club. 'Gary, what's the score?' chimed the travelling fans.

For so much of the contest, Ipswich looked composed and confident on the ball, played with energy and intent and, after they pulled one back, showed how much pressure they can put teams under and how much this place can bounce.

They are a much better side than the one that came up last time but you cannot come out after the break and have Ouattara give the ball straight to Evanilson again inside 30 seconds as he did before Ryan Christie's shot took two deflections and went in.

'Gutted,' said O'Neil. 'To lose a game that you haven't been outclassed is tough to take. We restricted Bournemouth to nothing of their own doing. If you give the ball to the opposition number nine twice, it's going to be difficult.'

#2013. Premier League KMI panel issues emphatic verdict on Alexander Isak penalty decision v Arsenal

The Premier League’s Key Match Incidents (KMI) Panel has concluded that Liverpool should’ve had a penalty awarded for an offence by Jurrien Timber on Alexander Isak in their defeat to Arsenal earlier this month.

Five minutes after Kai Havertz scored the only goal of the game at Anfield, the Swedish striker had his shirt pulled in the box by the Gunners defender, but neither on-field referee Andy Madley nor Stuart Attwell on VAR felt compelled to award a spot kick despite the transgression being clear.

The Reds’ head coach Andoni Iraola went as far as claiming that a penalty would’ve been awarded had our number 9 gone to ground instead of staying on his feet when his jersey was grabbed.

On Wednesday, the Premier League published the findings of several incidents reviewed by the KMI Panel, including the one involving Isak and Timber on 1 November.

Their verdict reads (via premierleague.com): ‘The panel felt that a penalty should have been awarded for a holding action by Timber on Isak, 4:1. One panellist considered the short-lived holding to lack clear impact on the ability of Isak to progress.

‘The majority also felt that VAR should have intervened to recommend an on-field review, 3:2, on the basis that it was a clear and obvious error. Two panellists considered that the subjectivity in assessing impact meant this did not meet the high threshold for VAR intervention.’

The KMI Panel concluded: ‘In this instance the panel deemed that Timber’s challenge on Isak met the threshold for a holding offence and should have resulted in a penalty kick, both on-field and through VAR intervention.’

Want more Empire of the Kop coverage? Add us as a preferred source on Google to your favourites list for news you can trust

How nice of the KMI Panel to come back and tell us what was so damn obvious at the time of the incident – or at least obvious to anyone not named Andy Madley or Stuart Attwell, or whichever member of the panel felt that the right decision was made on the day.

How that individual concluded that Timber’s actions lacked ‘clear impact on the ability of Isak to progress’ is baffling – the Liverpool striker would surely have gotten on the end of Bradley Barcola’s cross had his shirt not been so blatantly pulled.

The panel’s verdict today won’t come as much consolation to anyone involved with the Reds, who were deprived of a legitimate penalty which – if converted – could’ve significantly altered the course of a match that they lost 1-0.

It’s not much good being told in retrospect that the officials got it wrong; these are clear decisions that professional referees should be capable of getting correct at the time, especially when they have the fallback option of VAR.

We get that many incidents are subjective and that consensus will never be achieved when it comes to refereeing in the Premier League, but there’s simply no excuse for botching calls like the Timber/Isak incident 10 days ago.

The issue is what will they do about the lost points. We all know it was a penalty except for Arsenal fans. Will these apologies bring back lost points?

Are they going to deduct points from Arsenal then? All talk , no action.

#2012. Liverpool played like a team fighting for their manager, but Pierre Sage looks like a dead man walking, writes LEWIS STEELE - as Reds clinch morale-boosting win at sorry Crystal Palace

Published: 11:14 EST, 8 November 2026 | Updated: 13:00 EST, 8 November 2026

By this time of the season, spirited performances mean little if you don't have the results to go with it.

Pierre Sage, who was sacked at Lyon two years ago, knows as much as anyone that this is a results-based business.

And he simply has not had enough results. Despite having Liverpool on the ropes at times here, Crystal Palace failed to land a knockout blow and that could be that for their under-fire manager, who looked like a dead man walking when he trudged off the pitch at full-time with a face like thunder.

Former Lens over-achiever Sage now seems set for a stuffing six weeks before Christmas and though he may curse at the small margins that denied his team a chance of a heavyweight and potential job-saving scalp here, the boss knows two wins in 10 league games is not good enough.

Liverpool, meanwhile, had the width of the crossbar and a throwback performance from goalkeeper Alisson to thank. In contrast to Sage, Andoni Iraola's side showed grit and determination to win when far from their best.

Alexis Mac Allister, Florian Wirtz and Alexander Isak all scored as the Reds put a tough week behind them that saw them lose back-to-back games for the first time in the Iraola era, which prompted a chorus of the old terrace classic 'Poetry in Motion'.

Florian Wirtz scored a rare Liverpool as they won 3-1 at Crystal Palace in the Premier League

Wirtz scored Liverpool's second on 54 minutes as they ran out as 3-1 winners at Selhurst Park

Things are looking ominous for under-pressure Palace manager Pierre Sage after another loss

This performance was hardly William Wordsworth levels of poetry and Liverpool were far from on song during large swathes of this match but when it really mattered, the attackers demonstrated just why the club spent so much money on them.

CRYSTAL PALACE (3-4-2-1): Henderson 5; Lerma 6, Richards 6, Disasi 5; Mingueza 6 (Khalali 87), Wharton 5, Timber 6 (Timber 60, 6), Mitchell 6; Kamada 6, Pino 7 (McNeil 87); Larsen 5 (Nketiah 72, 7)

Subs not used: Benitez, Canvot, Chilwell, Doucoure, Hughes

LIVERPOOL (4-2-3-1): Alisson 9; Araujo 7 (Gomez 90), Jacquet 6, Van Dijk 6, Kerkez 6; Szoboszlai 7 (Nyoni 69, 7), Mac Allister 8; Gakpo 6 (Ngumoha 76) Wirtz 8, Barcola 7 (Munoz 69, 7); Isak 7 (Koumas 90)

Subs not used: Mamardashvili, Endo, McConnell, Tsimikas

Booked: Araujo, Barcola, Munoz, Mac Allister

Scorers: Mac Allister 40, Wirtz 54, Isak 89

Mac Allister resumed his bemusing role of the team's best aerial threat despite being their smallest player, Wirtz got a goal and assist, while Isak made it eight for the season to continue his prolific streak.

Bradley Barcola, meanwhile, proved what an asset he is despite a wasteful first half.

Those attackers were worthy of praise but no one deserved plaudits more so than goalkeeper, Alisson, who was player of the match in an illustration of Palace's first-half supremacy.

'I'm very pleased with Alisson's performance,' said Iraola. 'He has commanded the box very well and in games here a lot of things are normally happening in the boxes. He has shown the level he has for us. Overall we are getting good results away from home at difficult stadiums.'

The Brazilian is in the last year of his contract but put in his best performance for 18 months, dating back to a 1-0 win at Paris Saint-Germain in the Champions League knockouts. He will not go on international duty and instead rest up after an injury-hit few years.

He denied Adam Wharton with a glancing header, thwarted Daichi Kamada with a fierce shot and then tipped round Quenten Timber's effort from distance. Palace also rattled the bar through Yeremy Pino in a first half that really should have ended up differently.

Jorgen Strand Larsen also had the ball in the net but was offside.

As it was, though, Liverpool were the team to take their chance when it came after a period of dilly-dallying and playing the wrong ball, guilty again of indecisiveness similar to the flaws shown against Arsenal last weekend and in the 3-2 defeat at Fenerbahce in midweek.

Liverpool led on 40 minutes when Alexis Mac Allister (centre left) scored from close range

The Argentine celebrates after breaking the deadlock for the Reds in the Premier League clash

Crystal Palace manager Pierre Sage is facing the sack after his side dropped to the bottom of the Premier League.

Palace have won just two of their ten league matches this season, with Sunday's 3-1 defeat to Liverpool leaving them at the foot of the league for the first time in nearly nine years.

Sage is expected to lose his job during the international break, with Sean Dyche and Thomas Frank leading the race to replace the French coach.

However, Sage believes his side have been unlucky with results this season and has requested the hierarchy remain patient.

The 47-year-old, who left RC Lens for Palace in the summer to succeed Oliver Glasner, also admitted the Palace squad needs strengthening - perhaps to absolve himself of some blame.

'You can create the links between these two things,' Sage replied when asked whether being bottom of the league heading into the international break could see him sacked.

'But a lot of times I've said we deserved better and it was the case again on Sunday.

'My job is not the most important thing, as I always said from the beginning. The most important thing is to find an efficient solution for the team and for the club.

'I know how important it is for the club to stay in the Premier League. The club just have to believe in that, and if it's not the case, they will take a decision.

'I always have confidence in myself because it's a big, big mistake to not be 100% involved in what I have to do.

'We have to adjust some positions during the winter transfer window to give more solutions and more efficiency and I think it will be okay.'

Mac Allister was the scorer as he continued a fine resurgence this season, with Dominik Szoboszlai the supplier after a week where he too had been criticised. The Hungarian whipped a cross towards Mac Allister, which was glanced past Henderson for 1-0.

The former Brighton player ran straight towards the Palace fans behind the goal and taunted the supporters that were once his rivals on the south coast.

Liverpool weathered another storm at the start of the second half and soon found themselves two up. Barcola, who had left lots to be desired in the first half, swapped wings at the break and made his first attack count.

The Frenchman put the after-burners on and motored down the pitch before feeding Wirtz, who composed himself and passed into the net for 2-0. Iraola praised the run of Isak which took him away from the ball but dragged defenders with him to create space for his colleague.

Isak squandered a one-versus-one chance not long after but was not going to miss another one minutes later, when a blisteringly quick counter-attack was started by Trey Nyoni and ended with Wirtz feeding Isak, who skipped past Chris Richards and finished calmly.

The three goals will delight the hierarchy, with all three of the £100m boys – Isak, Barcola and Wirtz – registering at least one goal or assist apiece, one each in Wirtz's case.

Alexander Isak scored the visitors' third in the 89th-minute with this right-footed finish

Eddie Nketiah pulled one back for Palace from the penalty in second-half stoppage time

This victory would not have been possible, though, without Alisson, now 34 and in the final year of his deal. For all the attacking talent at Iraola's disposal, the Basque will be delighted at his team's defensive determination when under the kosh here as Palace had 10 first-half shots.

Iraola knows his team has flaws and they remain a work-in-progress. But despite a few challenging afternoons, they appear to be heading in the right direction.

The same cannot be said for Sage, whose side pulled one back in stoppage time through an Eddie Nketiah penalty after Milos Kerkez committed a careless foul.

Palace were unlucky in this game but the cold, hard truth is that the recent FA Cup and Europa Conference League triumphs feel a world away now as they enter the international break rock bottom of the Premier League.

West Ham also won a European trophy in the last five years and look where they ended up — that should set alarm bells ringing that no success lasts for ever and Palace are not too big for relegation.

Nketiah's goal felt like it was too little, too late and the sage advice for Palace supremo Steve Parish might be a reluctant change in the dugout.
